title: Summary Ranges
directAnswer: The array is sorted and has no duplicates, so consecutive runs of integers form the ranges. Walk once: remember where the current run started, and whenever the next number is not exactly one more than the current (or you hit the end), close the run — emit `"a"` if it's a single number or `"a->b"` if it spans more than one. One linear pass, O(n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output.

remember.pattern: Single pass, track run start, close on a break in consecutiveness
remember.formula:
i = 0
while i < n:
    start = nums[i]
    while i + 1 < n and nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1: i += 1
    end = nums[i]
    out.append(str(start) if start == end else f"{start}->{end}")
    i += 1
rules: The input is **sorted and distinct** — that's the whole reason consecutive integers (`nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1`) define a range.
Compare with `nums[i] + 1`, **not** `nums[i+1] - nums[i] == 1` blindly across signed overflow — values fit in 32-bit but a `long`/careful compare avoids edge surprises at INT_MAX.
Emit `"a"` when `start == end`, else `"a->b"` — forgetting the single-element case produces `"5->5"`.
Advance the inner pointer **while** the run continues, then emit once — don't emit per element.
Handle the **empty array** up front: return an empty list, no ranges.
whenToUse: Compress a sorted, distinct integer array into consecutive ranges
'Group adjacent / consecutive runs' over already-ordered data
Summarize gaps in a sequence (the complement is Missing Ranges)
Any single-pass run-length style scan over sorted input
antiSignals: Array is unsorted → sort first, or this consecutiveness test is meaningless
Duplicates allowed → the `+1` test breaks; you'd need run-length on equal values instead
You need to MERGE overlapping [start,end] intervals → that's Merge Intervals, sort by start and sweep
You must find which numbers are missing → Missing Ranges, scan the gaps not the runs
remember.takeaway: Summary Ranges is the gentlest 'scan a sorted array and group consecutive elements' problem. The reusable idea: when input is pre-sorted, a single pass that detects 'breaks' (where the next element stops being consecutive) turns into ranges, run-lengths, or gap reports — the same skeleton powers Missing Ranges and run-length encoding.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the 'sorted, no duplicates' precondition to do one clean linear pass, and whether you correctly handle the single-element range formatting and the empty input.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Emitting `"5->5"` for a lone number instead of `"5"`, or building ranges with an off-by-one that drops the last run or double-counts boundaries.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the precondition out loud ('sorted + distinct ⇒ consecutive integers form runs'), handle empty up front, and mention the sibling problem Missing Ranges to show you see the pattern family.

problemStatement:
You are given a **sorted unique** integer array `nums`.

A *range* `[a,b]` is the set of all integers from `a` to `b` (inclusive).

Return the **smallest sorted** list of ranges that **cover all the numbers in the array exactly**. That is, each element of `nums` is covered by exactly one of the ranges, and there is no integer `x` such that `x` is in one of the ranges but not in `nums`.

Each range `[a,b]` in the list should be output as:

- `"a->b"` if `a != b`
- `"a"` if `a == b`
constraints: All the values of nums are unique
nums is sorted in ascending order
understanding: Given an already sorted array with no repeats, group maximal stretches of consecutive integers into ranges. A stretch is consecutive when each value is exactly one greater than the previous. Output each stretch as a single number if it has length one, otherwise as `start->end`. The array may be empty.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array guaranteed sorted and free of duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the prompt says 'sorted unique'. That precondition is what lets `nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1` define a range; without it I'd have to sort and dedupe first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes (length can be 0). I'll return an empty list immediately for that case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative or at the 32-bit extremes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, values span the full int range including INT_MIN and INT_MAX. I'll compare against `nums[i] + 1` carefully so I don't overflow at the top end.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should a single number be formatted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: As just `"a"`, not `"a->a"`. That single-element case is the main formatting trap.

approaches.whenToMention: This is the answer for an easy problem — go straight to it after noting the sorted+distinct precondition.
hints: The array is sorted with no duplicates. What does it mean, then, when nums[i+1] is exactly nums[i] + 1 versus when it jumps by more?
Remember where the current consecutive run started. Keep extending while the next element is one bigger; the moment it isn't, you've found the end of a range.
When you close a range, emit "start" if start equals end, otherwise "start->end". Then start a fresh run at the next element.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each element is visited exactly once by the combined outer/inner pointer advancement → O(n) time. Only a few scalar variables are used; the output list isn't counted as extra working space → O(1) auxiliary space.
approaches.explanation:
Because the array is **sorted and contains no duplicates**, a maximal range is precisely a maximal run of consecutive integers — values where each is exactly one more than the one before. The algorithm is a single left-to-right scan that remembers where the current run began and detects the instant the run breaks.

**The core observation.** Sortedness alone isn't enough; the absence of duplicates is what makes `nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1` a clean test for 'still in the same range'. If duplicates were allowed, two equal values would have a difference of 0 and the test would mislead. With both guarantees, the only two transitions are: the sequence continues (`+1`) or it jumps (gap `> 1`), and a jump is exactly a range boundary.

**How the scan works.** We set `start = nums[i]` at the beginning of each run. Then we advance an inner pointer as long as the *next* element keeps the run consecutive. When that inner loop stops, `nums[i]` is the run's `end`. We emit the range — `"start"` when `start == end` (a lone number), otherwise `"start->end"` — then step past `end` to begin the next run. Repeating until the array is consumed produces every range in sorted order automatically, because the input was sorted to begin with.

**Why the single-element check matters.** The output spec is explicit: a lone number is `"5"`, not `"5->5"`. This is the single most common bug on this problem. Comparing `start` and `end` before formatting handles it cleanly. The other classic slip is an off-by-one — emitting per element instead of per run, or forgetting to emit the final run after the loop ends; structuring the loop as 'extend while consecutive, then emit once' avoids both.

**Overflow caution at the extremes.** Values can be `INT_MAX`. Writing the consecutiveness test as `nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1` is fine in Python (arbitrary precision) but in Java `nums[i] + 1` could overflow if `nums[i]` were `INT_MAX` — though since the array is strictly increasing, a value equal to `INT_MAX` can only be the last element, so `nums[i+1]` wouldn't exist. Still, comparing as `(long) nums[i] + 1` or checking `nums[i+1] - nums[i] != 1` with care is the defensive habit worth voicing.
approaches.insight: Pre-sorted input is a gift: it converts 'group consecutive elements' into a single forward scan that detects breaks. The same skeleton — remember the start, extend while a predicate holds, emit on break — generalizes to run-length encoding, Missing Ranges (emit the gaps instead of the runs), and counting contiguous segments.

pitfalls: Formatting a single number as "a->a" instead of "a".
Off-by-one that drops the final run — make sure the emit happens after the inner loop, every iteration.
Testing nums[i+1] - nums[i] == 1 in Java where the subtraction could overflow at extremes — prefer nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1 or use long.

commonMistakes: Outputting "a->a" for a single-element range instead of "a".
Dropping the last range by emitting inside the wrong loop branch.
Assuming the array might be unsorted and over-engineering a sort.
Integer overflow when computing differences at INT_MAX in Java.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Formatting a lone number as "a->a"
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The spec says a single number must be "a", not "a->a". Always compare start and end before formatting.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: out.append(f"{start}->{end}")   # produces "5->5" for a single value
commonMistakesDetailed.good: out.append(str(start) if start == end else f"{start}->{end}")

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one that drops the last run
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only emit when you *see* a break, the final run (which ends at the array boundary, not a break) never gets emitted. Structure the loop to emit after each inner-extend completes.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow in the consecutiveness test
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In Java, nums[i] + 1 overflows if nums[i] == INT_MAX. Although a strictly increasing array can only hold INT_MAX as its last element (so the +1 is never reached), defensive code uses long or compares as nums[i+1] == nums[i] + 1 only when i+1 exists.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: while (i + 1 < n && nums[i + 1] - nums[i] == 1 && nums[i] == Integer.MAX_VALUE) { /* fragile */ }

patternNote: Single-pass run detection over a sorted, distinct array. Recognize it when pre-sorted input lets you group consecutive elements by detecting 'breaks' where the next element stops being one greater. The same scan, with the emit logic flipped to the gaps, solves Missing Ranges; generalized to [start,end] pairs it becomes the Merge Intervals family.
